passage: On the bus home in Stockholm, Ingrid was telling Rafael about her future again. "I'm going to be a surgeon. Heart surgery, like in that documentary. I'll work in a big hospital, maybe travel to places that need doctors." Rafael nodded. "Cool. So what are you doing for it this month?" Ingrid opened her mouth. "Well... I mean, I'll study." "Study what, though? You said you hate chemistry." "I'll get to it." She looked out of the window. Her biology test was in two weeks. She hadn't opened the chapter. The dream felt so bright and so far away that there was nothing to do about it today.

Sonali stared at the blank lines, feeling both deflated and oddly relieved.

Counsellor's note, Class 11, Wednesday.
Mridul came in today for the career session and said, with great confidence, that he is going to be a neurosurgeon at a top government hospital. When I asked what he's doing this month towards it, he talked about a documentary he'd watched and a surgeon he follows online. He didn't know his current biology mark, which is 54 percent, or which entrance exam he would take, or when it is held. He isn't lazy; the dream clearly matters to him, and his eyes light up when he talks about it. But it's floating with nothing tying it to his week. We worked together on a one-month plan: two biology chapters with self-tests, one practice set every Saturday, and a talk with his chemistry teacher about weak areas. He copied it into his phone. Follow-up: meet again on the 30th to check progress.
Nilesh

In Khandala village, Seema was known as the girl who wanted to be a doctor. She said it at every wedding. The school headmaster said it too, proudly.
But every evening she sat on the charpai, notebook open, and did nothing in particular. The dream was so big she didn't know where to put her pencil.

Seema opened her mouth. Nothing came.
Zeenat Didi pulled out a scrap of paper. “Class 10 science. The board exam is in five months. This month: finish the chapter on life processes. Every day, one page, with diagrams. That's step one.”
Seema stared at the paper. It was tiny. It was also the first thing she knew how to start.

passage: At the school career fair, Usha told the counsellor, Nazia ma'am, "I want to be a doctor." Nazia ma'am smiled. "Wonderful. What are you doing this month for it?" Usha blinked. She'd wanted to be a doctor since Class 5. She had a stethoscope keychain. But this month? "Studying," she said. "Which part?" Usha looked down. "I haven't really started. It feels so far away." Nazia ma'am pulled out a small planner. "A far dream is like a star. It tells you the direction. But you walk with small steps." Together they wrote three things for the month: finish two biology chapters, do one chemistry test paper each week, and talk to Usha's aunt, who is a nurse, about hospital life. Usha stared at the list. "That's it?" "For this month. Next month, three more." Usha left the fair holding the planner like a map.

Dear Bidisha didi,
You're the only doctor-in-training I know, so I'm writing to you. I'm in Class 10 and I want to be a doctor, like you. I tell everyone. I've even watched videos of surgeries.
But here's the problem. When Ma asked what I'm doing this month to get closer, I had nothing to say. I haven't finished the biology syllabus. I don't know which entrance exam I need or when. I just have this big dream and a lot of feelings about it.

Could you tell me what you did at my age, month by month? Even three small things would help. I think I need steps I can see from here, not just the finish line.
With love,
Reena
